radar.title: Multiagent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
radar.summary: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the two-sided assortment optimization model. Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform’s decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Because of the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily badly. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a [Formula: see text]-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a [Formula: see text]-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting, with both sides following MNL models. Finally, we assess the performance of our proposed methods with a detailed computational study and discuss several extensions. Funding: M. radar.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.
radar.summary_short: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive.

radar.title: Reframing decentralized diagnostics with a programmable multi-dimensional microfluidic system
The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
radar.summary: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, over 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

radar.title: Game theory driven multi-agent framework mitigates language model hallucination
radar.summary: Lightweight large language models hold promise for scientific applications but remain limited in rule-constrained domains because they can reproduce linguistic patterns without following scientific principles, leading to hallucinations. Here, we show that G-Frame, an adaptive multi-agent framework inspired by Bayesian game and team game principles, enables a closed-loop process for automated data generation, model evaluation, and training. By assigning complementary roles to multiple agents, G-Frame generates structured reasoning data and constructs a specialized corpus containing 363,045 chain-of-thought examples and 199,589 question–answer pairs. Using this corpus together with domain pre-training and adaptive training, the 7-billion-parameter model OmniChem achieves competitive performance across the reported benchmarks and reduces the ChemJudge hallucination rate from 41.95% for the base model to 12.91%. Case studies further illustrate potential applications in molecular design and selected synthesis-planning tasks. These results support G-Frame as an extensible game theory-driven multi-agent framework for improving the reliability of lightweight scientific language models. Lightweight AI models can be unreliable in specialized scientific tasks. Here, the authors introduce G-Frame, which uses game theory to coordinate multiple AI agents, automate data generation and training, and reduce hallucinations.

radar.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
radar.summary: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

The seller knows only an upper bound on these values and does not know their distribution. The objective is to devise a deterministic auction mechanism effective across a broad set of distributions. We propose a second price auction with a reserve price set at half of the upper bound. radar.title: Globally guided multi-agent reinforcement learning with decoupled critics for cooperative UAV path planning
radar.summary: Abstract Cooperative path planning for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) requires the simultaneous achievement of target navigation, collision avoidance, and formation coordination in complex obstacle environments. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods often suffer from sparse rewards, local deadlocks, and conflicts between formation maintenance and obstacle avoidance, which can destabilize policy learning. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Globally Guided Decoupled-Critic Multi-Agent Soft Actor-Critic algorithm (GDC-MASAC). RRT $$^*$$ -based global guidance provides reference waypoints for the leader UAV, reducing inefficient exploration and local deadlocks. Three decoupled Critic branches separately evaluate target navigation, formation maintenance, and safety objectives, while an environment-aware formation reward adjustment relaxes formation tracking near obstacles according to the distance to obstacle boundaries. Experiments under different obstacle densities and swarm sizes show that GDC-MASAC improves mission completion, collision avoidance, and formation coordination. In a scenario with 12 obstacles and 3 UAVs, GDC-MASAC achieves a mission success rate of 86%, whereas the baseline methods achieve success rates below 50%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of GDC-MASAC for cooperative multi-UAV path planning in cluttered environments.
radar.summary_short: Abstract Cooperative path planning for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) requires the simultaneous achievement of target navigation, collision avoidance, and formation coordination in complex obstacle environments.

radar.title: Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Control of Multiple Unmanned Surface Vehicle in Neutralizing Threat Vessels
radar.venue: Journal of Institute of Control Robotics and Systems
radar.venue_raw: Journal of Institute of Control Robotics and Systems
radar.summary: This study proposes a cooperative capture system in which two allied unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) jointly deploy a capture net to intercept noncooperative vessels in naval environments. To overcome the limitations of traditional rule-based methods subjected to environmental uncertainties, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework is developed within a high-fidelity, unity-based simulation environment incorporating the Gerstner wave and wind disturbance models. Each agent utilizes an egocentric polar coordinate observation space; distance values are normalized via a nonlinear rational function to prioritize close-range sensitivity, while angular discontinuities are resolved through trigonometric transformations. The Multi-Agent POsthumous Credit Assignment algorithm is adopted within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution architecture, enabling robust strategy learning through posthumous credit assignment even when agents exit the environment. The reward structure is designed hierarchically, combining sparse event rewards for capture success with dense continuous rewards based on formation maintenance, target approach, and heading alignment. Quantitative experimental results demonstrate that the proposed MARL-based approach significantly outperforms the modified Line-of-Sight guidance law, achieving a 65% capture success rate and a three-fold reduction in formation collapse under dynamic sea conditions. This study confirms that the proposed framework effectively enables autonomous USVs to learn complex, coordinated maneuvers for physical maritime interdiction, providing a robust solution for securing maritime security.
radar.summary_short: This study proposes a cooperative capture system in which two allied unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) jointly deploy a capture net to intercept noncooperative vessels in naval environments.

radar.title: Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange
radar.summary: Unlocking Value Through Nonprofit Resource Sharing Nonprofit organizations often operate under tight budgets while idle equipment, unused space, and shareable skills and expertise are frequently underutilized, with existing resource exchanges in the nonprofit sector limited to bilateral barter or relatively homogeneous resources. In “Community-Oriented Market Design for Nonprofit Resource Exchange,” Huang et al. propose Sharing With a Purpose (SWAP), a resource-sharing system that enables nonprofits to exchange heterogeneous resources without monetary payments. SWAP combines an auction-based process, SWAPcredit valuation, and integer optimization to facilitate multilateral exchanges, allowing nonprofits to obtain needed resources by contributing resources of their own. The authors implement this market design through the SWAP Hub, a digital platform deployed with nonprofit communities in multiple regions. Through repeated exchange episodes, participating organizations have shared not only physical assets but also a wide range of skills, services, and expertise, including marketing, management, event planning, and organizational development. The study demonstrates how innovative market design can unlock latent value in community resources, alleviate resource constraints, and encourage new connections and collaboration among nonprofit organizations.

radar.title: Emergent collaborative scheduling in satellite swarms: A distributed multi-agent reinforcement learning approach with adaptive experience evolution
radar.summary: Autonomous collaboration among multiple Earth observation satellites is essential for improving the performance of satellite swarms. However, this task is challenging because of limited onboard computing resources and unstable inter-satellite links, particularly when global coordination is required under communication constraints. Traditional centralized optimization methods often adapt poorly to dynamic observation requests, whereas existing multi-agent approaches may incur communication overhead that hinders practical deployment. To address this issue, we propose a distributed scheduling framework that enables emergent global coordination through local agent interactions and formulates the problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP). Specifically, we develop L-QTRAN, a multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that enables satellites to coordinate based on local observations with limited communication. To alleviate the non-stationarity inherent in dynamic swarm environments, we introduce an Adaptive Experience Evolution (AEE) mechanism. This mechanism follows the survival-of-the-fittest principle by selectively retaining elite transition experiences, thereby accelerating the development of cooperative strategies. Furthermore, a Random Segment Sampling (RSS) technique is introduced to improve training stability and convergence in high-dimensional solution spaces. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms the baseline methods under weak-communication conditions and achieves sub-second response times, highlighting its potential for autonomous satellite swarms operating in dynamic environments.

radar.title: Single and multi-winner auctions with performance obligation
Uniform-Price Mechanism Design for Automated Market Makers
radar.summary: Automated market makers (AMMs) are central to decentralized exchanges, but their reserve curves make mechanism design different from classical double auctions. We study a batch double auction with buyers, sellers, and a liquidity-nondecreasing AMM: post-trade reserves must have weakly larger product than the initial reserves. Each user has two-dimensional private information: a unit value and a demand or supply quantity. User trades clear at one uniform price subject to AMM feasibility. The objective is user-side trading volume, benchmarked against the optimal feasible individually rational (IR) uniform-price allocation. We give a randomized uniform-price mechanism based on binary quantity buckets. It randomly chooses one of three clearing modes: peer-to-peer matching, AMM sales to buyers, and seller sales to the AMM. Every deterministic realization of the mechanism is ex-post feasible and satisfies IR and weak quantity incentive compatibility: conditional on any quantity report, truthful unit-value reporting is dominant whenever it gives a non-negative utility, no unit-value deviation gives a positive utility if the truthful one doesn't, and users cannot benefit by under-reporting the quantity together with their truthful unit value. Let $V^\ast$ be the optimal feasible IR uniform-price volume without incentive constraints, and let $γ=\bar q/\underline q$, where $\bar q$ and $\underline q$ are the quantity-domain bounds. For $γ\ge1$, the mechanism achieves an expected trading volume of $ Ω(1/(1+\logγ)^2)V^\ast - O(\bar q). $ We also show that full incentive compatibility over the two-dimensional type space forces a worst-case approximation ratio of $O(1/γ)$ at every prescribed initial reserve ratio, even when both AMM reserves are scaled by an arbitrarily large common factor and the optimal volume $V^\ast$ is arbitrarily large relative to $\bar q$.

radar.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Evaluating and Mitigating Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
radar.summary: In the world of large language models (LLMs), prompt injection attacks are a severe security risk that can circumvent the instructions given to AI agents and potentially cause damage. In agentic architectures, the vulnerabilities are magnified because of the increased attack surfaces which are present in the use of tools, APIs and chains of reasoning. The vulnerabilities are compounded in agentic architectures as the tools used, APIs called, and chains of reasoning become a larger attack surface, resulting in an increased sense of unreliability. Paraphrased, adaptive, and context-aware attacks are not thwarted by rule-based and static prompt engineering defenses. This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to detecting and thwarting prompt injection attacks in LLM agent systems. Uses a hybrid model of known and customer-generated adversarial prompts to combine transformer-based classification, semantic risk-scoring and adaptive mitigation procedures. Stratified data splits are used in the experiments, as are synthetic attack generation and rule-based, BERT and zero-shot LLM classifiers. In terms of precision, recall, F1 score and AUC, the proposed framework is found to be better than all the baselines. Attack of instruction override, data extraction and tool misuse are greatly enhanced and resistant to adversarial scenarios that are not seen and adaptable. The mitigation module achieves high task utility; low false positive rates and the high success rate of the attacks is significantly reduced. Overall, the framework demonstrates that it is possible to integrate detection, risk estimation, and mitigation in a single pipeline, resulting in a great improvement in the security of LLM agents, while not burdening them with significant computing costs. It further highlights the importance of security layers before deploying LLM agents to the real world as the input they receive can be adversarial and continuously change, requiring a mixture of machine learning and structured control to ensure they remain safe and reliable across different application areas. Scalable AI systems deployment safety improvements involve multi-agent security, real-time learning, and multimodal prompt injection detection in the future.

radar.title: Context-Aware Cooperative Gating for Knowledge-Controlled Value Factorization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.venue: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
radar.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial observability requires decentralized agents to act from incomplete local information. Value-decomposition methods such as VDN and QMIX do not control when teammate-related knowledge may influence an agent’s local utility, and an uncontrolled teammate-conditioned term can distort decisions at timesteps where no ally is observable. We propose CA-QMIX, a context-aware value factorization method that uses ally visibility as a knowledge signal for decentralized agent control. Each agent combines an individual decision branch with an attention-based cooperative knowledge branch through a visibility-conditioned gate that scales the cooperative contribution and is hard-masked to zero when no ally is observable. The gated utilities are combined by a QMIX-style monotonic mixer, which we prove preserves Individual-Global-Max consistency, and a mixer-level Δ-Q regularizer discourages cooperative corrections that lower the greedy value of the base branch. Experiments on seven SMAC v1 and SMAC v2 scenarios against six value-decomposition baselines show that CA-QMIX attains the highest mean final win rate and the best mean rank over the seven scenarios and improves on QMIX in all three randomized SMAC v2 scenarios. Ablations show that most of the gain comes from the cooperative branch, that its visibility conditioning helps when correctly aligned (misaligned visibility degrades performance under randomized placement), and that the form of the gate is not critical: a binary gate suffices and the hard no-ally mask has no measurable cost.

In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?
radar.summary: When Learning About a Match Stalls the Market In many matching markets, participants must investigate whether a match is feasible. When inspection is costly, participants may delay investigating a potential match until both sides have effectively committed. Such caution can cause each side to wait for others to act, creating an “information deadlock.” In their article, “In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?” Immorlica, Kanoria, and Lu study this problem in random two-sided markets. They characterize how deadlock depends on the market balance, market connectivity, and the chance that inspections succeed. Using statistical physics tools, their analysis identifies phase transitions between deadlock-free and deadlocked markets. The findings offer design guidance: More choice is not always better; match rates are highest at the deadlock phase boundary; and parallel inspections and clearer participant differentiation can reduce the extent to which waiting chains stall the market.
radar.summary_short: When Learning About a Match Stalls the Market In many matching markets, participants must investigate whether a match is feasible. When inspection is costly, participants may delay investigating a potential match until both sides have effectively committed.

radar.title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
radar.summary: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04789 .

radar.title: Autonomous biomedical research with an artificial intelligence agent
radar.summary: Biomedical research is increasingly constrained by repetitive, fragmented workflows that slow discovery. We introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical artificial intelligence agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks. To map the biomedical action space, Biomni’s action-discovery agent mines tools, databases, and protocols from thousands of publications across 25 domains, building a unified agentic environment. Its general-purpose architecture integrates large language model reasoning with retrieval-augmented planning and code-based execution, dynamically composing workflows without predefined templates. Systematic benchmarking shows strong generalization across heterogeneous tasks—causal gene prioritization, drug repurposing, rare-disease diagnosis, microbiome analysis, and molecular cloning—without task-specific tuning. Real-world case studies demonstrate Biomni interpreting multimodal datasets, optimizing protein stability, orchestrating wet-lab instruments, and generating experimentally testable protocols. Biomni envisions artificial intelligence augmenting human scientists and accelerating discovery.

radar.title: Constant Regret Primal-Dual Policy for Multiway Dynamic Matching
radar.summary: We study a discrete-time dynamic multiway matching model. There are finitely many agent types that arrive stochastically and wait to be matched. State-of-the-art dynamic matching policies in the literature require the knowledge of all system parameters to determine an optimal basis of the fluid relaxation, and focus on controlling the number of waiting agents using only matches within the optimal basis. In this paper, we propose a primal-dual policy that schedules matches for future arrivals based on an estimator for the dual solution. Our policy does not require the knowledge of the arrival rates and operates with greater flexibility as it does not restrict matches to only the match types within an optimal basis. We show that our policy is the first to achieve constant regret at all times under unknown arrival rates, and when the arrival rates are known, it achieves the optimal scaling. Furthermore, when the arrival rates are known, the primal-dual policy significantly outperforms alternative dynamic matching policies in several numerical simulations. radar.title: Active multi-view selection for UAV-satellite remote sensing image matching using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Cross-view image matching between unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellite platforms has emerged as a fundamental technique for vision-based geo-localization and GNSS-denied navigation. While utilizing multi-view fusion can improve retrieval accuracy by providing comprehensive scene information, it also incurs a cost that grows with the number of processed views and may introduce correlated or ambiguous observations. Importantly, the benefit of selection is altitude dependent: reducing the view set does not universally improve top-rank accuracy, and the principal advantage is an accuracy–efficiency trade-off rather than uniform superiority over full fusion. To address this issue, we propose MARL-AVSF, an efficient Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework designed for active multi-view selection. Instead of passively fusing all captured images, MARL-AVSF deploys a cooperative multi-agent system to intelligently select a minimal subset of highly complementary viewpoints. Extensive experiments on the multi-height SUES-200 remote sensing benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. By actively selecting only three critical views, MARL-AVSF achieves a Recall@1 of 77.50% at 200 m, compared with 75.00% for the 50-view full-fusion baseline, while reducing the number of processed views by 94%. Across all four altitudes, the method improves mean Average Precision from 81.79% to 84.34%, but its mean Recall@1 is 3.13% points lower than full fusion; at 150 m, the Recall@1 deficit is 10.00 points. These results qualify the claim: selection improves ranking quality and efficiency on average, whereas its top-rank advantage is specific to 200 m.
radar.summary_short: Cross-view image matching between unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellite platforms has emerged as a fundamental technique for vision-based geo-localization and GNSS-denied navigation.

radar.title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
radar.summary: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent's own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent's shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.
radar.summary_short: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy.

radar.title: Dynamic Contract Design with Learning
radar.summary: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable. In “Dynamic Contract Design with Learning,” Wang, Liang, and Sun study the interaction between learning and moral hazard: effort is costly and unobservable, so a missing arrival may reflect an unfavorable market, bad luck, or shirking. The firm’s goal is to design a dynamic contract governing arrival-based payments and termination, thereby motivating effort while learning whether to continue. Yet shirking can make the principal more pessimistic than the agent and create scope to manipulate future payments. The authors prove that an optimal contract inducing full effort until termination exists, but computing it appears prohibitively complex. They develop two simple online contracts with payments and termination thresholds fixed in advance. Both induce full effort and achieve O(ln T) regret over T periods against a first-best, full-information benchmark. A matching Ω(ln T) lower bound proves rate optimality. The results extend to continuous time and differing prior beliefs.
radar.summary_short: Incentivizing Effort While Learning the Market Condition When a firm hires an agent to generate customers in a new market, neither party initially knows whether the market is favorable.

radar.title: Who Directs the Control Tower? Customer vs. Supplier-Managed Inventory in Supply Chains
radar.summary: Information distortion and incentive misalignment often undermine supply chain performance. In response, many firms adopt a “control tower” approach, whereby one party assumes responsibility for replenishment decisions across the supply chain. Industry examples showed that this role may be assigned to the customer, Customer-Managed Inventory (CMI), or to the supplier, Supplier-Managed Inventory (SMI). This paper investigates when one governance structure is preferable. We study a two-echelon, one-to-many supply chain consisting of a single supplier and a customer operating multiple warehouses. We characterize optimal base-stock policies and equilibrium holding-cost-sharing parameters under CMI and SMI and benchmark them against decentralized operations and a fully centralized system. Two primary forces shape the choice between CMI and SMI: the relative shortage penalty costs of the two parties and the structure of the customer’s distribution network. Specifically, CMI is preferred when the customer faces relatively higher shortage penalties and operates in a more asymmetric environment—for example, when demand is concentrated in a subset of its warehouses or when replenishment lead times vary substantially across these locations. In contrast, SMI is favored under opposite conditions. We further examine how intertemporal and interspatial demand correlations affect this comparison. A key finding is that, although neither CMI nor SMI achieves the first-best outcome, their efficiency loss relative to full centralization is typically small. Calibrated numerical studies based on four industry cases disentangle the incremental value of information sharing, decision-right transfer, and cost sharing, showing that most performance gains stem from decision-right transfer supported by appropriate holding-cost sharing. EcoTrust-Net: A Causal, Explainable, and Energy-Aware Graph Transformer and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Intelligent Network Traffic Prediction and Optimization
radar.summary: The increasing complexity of sixth-generation (6G) communication systems, Software-Defined Networking (SDN), edge intelligence, cloud-native infrastructures, and Internet of Things (IoT) environments has intensified the need for intelligent network traffic prediction and optimization capable of supporting low latency, high throughput, cyber-resilience, explainability, and energy-efficient operation. Existing approaches often address traffic prediction, routing optimization, explainability, or energy efficiency independently, resulting in limited topology awareness, weak causal interpretation, and reduced adaptability in highly dynamic communication environments. To address these limitations, this study proposes EcoTrust-Net, a causal, explainable, and energy-aware framework that integrates Graph Transformer-based topologyaware traffic prediction, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for adaptive routing and congestion control, Structural Causal Modeling (SCM) for causal inference and counterfactual reasoning, SHAP- and attention-based explainability, and multi-objective energy-aware optimization within a unified architecture. The framework was evaluated using heterogeneous datasets and environments comprising CAIDA backbone traffic traces, CIC-DDoS2019 attack traffic, Alibaba Cluster Trace workload data and NS-3/Mininet SDN simulations. Comparative experiments against conventional methods and recent state-of-the-art models published between 2024 and 2026, together with component-level ablation analysis, were conducted to assess prediction accuracy, Quality of Service (QoS), explainability, cyber-resilience and energy efficiency. Under the experimental conditions evaluated, EcoTrust-Net achieved 97.4% prediction accuracy, 96.8% precision, 96.1% recall, 96.4% F1-score, and an RMSE of 2.1. The framework also achieved 781 Mbps throughput, 12.4 ms latency, 1.8% packet loss, 97.1% attack detection, a 2.3% false-positive rate and 187 W energy consumption, outperforming the selected baseline models. These findings suggest that integrating topology-aware graph learning, cooperative reinforcement learning, causal reasoning, explainable artificial intelligence, and energy-aware optimization provides a promising framework for scalable, interpretable, and sustainable intelligent network traffic prediction and optimization in next-generation AI native communication networks.

radar.title: CocoRNA: Collective RNA Design with Cooperative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Designing RNA sequences that reliably fold into specific secondary structures is essential for understanding their biological functions but remains a challenging computational problem. We propose CocoRNA, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for RNA inverse design. CocoRNA simplifies the design task by decomposing it into smaller sub-problems, each solved collaboratively by multiple agents. This approach reduces the complexity of the problem and improves the exploration of design policies. During training, a centralized critic uses global structural information to guide the agents, enabling them to jointly optimize their design strategies. As a result, CocoRNA learns high-quality RNA design policies that generalize effectively to unseen structures without additional training. Experiments on the Rfam dataset demonstrate that CocoRNA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both success rate and design speed. Further experiments on other biological sequence design tasks highlight the effectiveness and broad potential of CocoRNA for complex design tasks.

radar.title: Supply Chain Resilience Optimization Integrating Transformers and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.venue: ICST Transactions on Scalable Information Systems
radar.venue_raw: ICST Transactions on Scalable Information Systems
radar.summary: INTRODUCTION: Manufacturing supply chains face increasing vulnerabilities from delayed risk identification, conflicting node-level decisions, and escalating recovery costs, particularly under complex disruption scenarios. Existing approaches often lack proactive, coordinated responses across autonomous supply chain nodes, limiting their ability to anticipate disruptions and synchronize mitigation actions effectively. To address these gaps, this paper proposes an integrated resilience optimization framework that combines predictive analytics with multi-agent coordination. OBJECTIVES: The primary objective is to develop a supply chain resilience framework, termed T-MARL, that enables autonomous suppliers, manufacturers, warehousing nodes, and distributors to: (1) predict future disruption probabilities using temporal risk precursor data, and (2) execute coordinated, proactive replenishment, production, and distribution decisions under inventory and capacity constraints. The framework aims to improve resilience index, reduce total operating costs, and shorten recovery time compared to baseline strategies, while also examining the sensitivity of performance gains to prediction noise and communication latency. METHODS: The T-MARL framework models each supply chain node as an independent agent. A lightweight Transformer captures temporal features from 6-dimensional risk precursor sequences over 12 consecutive periods to forecast disruption probabilities. These predictions feed into a value-decomposition multi-agent reinforcement learning mechanism with centralized training–decentralized execution, where a value-decomposition network orchestrates cross-node actions. Risk-constrained action gating ensures that proactive responses adhere to inventory and capacity limits. A digital twin simulation environment was built with fixed random seeds, covering three scenarios—single-source supply disruption, demand surge, and compound disruption. Five strategies were tested, with 30 runs per unit using common random number pairing. RESULTS: On the trajectory-held-out test set, the Transformer achieved an AUC of 0.722 and an F1-score of 0.586, while Random Forest achieved a slightly higher AUC of 0.724. Under the compound disruption scenario, T-MARL attained a resilience index of 0.849—a 1.63 percentage-point gain over VDN-MARL -reduced total cost by 14.7%, and shortened average recovery time from 1.67 periods to zero. T-MARL also achieved lower operating costs while maintaining service levels comparable to rule-based strategies. However, the paper also found that prediction noise and communication latency diminish these performance gains. CONCLUSION: This research contributes a reproducible digital twin analysis framework for disruption prediction, cross-node collaborative response, and rapid recovery in manufacturing supply chains. While T-MARL demonstrates significant improvements in resilience and cost-efficiency under ideal conditions, practical deployment must account for real-world imperfections such as noisy forecasts and delayed communications. The framework provides a scalable foundation for future work on adaptive, data-driven supply chain resilience.

radar.title: Large language model multiagent systems for industrial problem discovery and prioritization
radar.summary: Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper. The benefits identified are presented as hypotheses for that agenda to test rather than as demonstrated outcomes.

radar.title: Evolutionary-assisted multi-agent reinforcement learning for waste electrical and electronic equipment inventory optimization under uncertainty
radar.summary: Waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) inventory optimization has attracted increasing attention with the growing emphasis on circular economy and sustainable development concepts. Effective uncertainty management is crucial for inventory optimization because recycling quantities fluctuate and custom order demands can arise unexpectedly. Although single-agent reinforcement learning methods can learn control policies for sequential decision-making tasks, they neglect collaboration and information sharing among multiple entities, making the resulting solutions unreliable in practical applications. In this paper, an evolutionary-assisted multi-agent reinforcement learning (EAMARL) method is proposed to achieve multi-period, multi-echelon WEEE supply chain inventory optimization. Specifically, a control model is proposed for WEEE inventory optimization under uncertain recycling quantities and custom order demands. The model integrates make-to-order (MTO) and make-to-stock (MTS) production modes, and the resulting optimization problem is formulated as a decentralized Markov decision process. A multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithm interacts with the WEEE supply chain environment to train control policies that maximize total profit. To address unstable convergence and limited exploration in MARL approaches, EAMARL integrates a population-based evolutionary algorithm that provides diverse exploratory experiences to support the training of MARL agents. Experiments in open-loop and closed-loop WEEE supply chain networks show that EAMARL improves average profit over the best-performing baseline by 12.09% and 14.39%, respectively. The normalized area under the learning curve of EAMARL indicates high learning efficiency and favorable convergence performance, while boxplot analysis demonstrates greater performance stability. Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and paired 95% confidence intervals further provide statistical support for the performance improvements.

radar.title: Federated Multiagent Soft Actor Critic for IRS Assisted Cognitive Radio Networks under Partial Observability
radar.summary: Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs) can improve spectrum efficiency and interference control in cognitive radio networks (CRNs) by reconfiguring the propagation environment. This paper presents FMASAC, a federated multi-agent soft actor-critic framework for IRS-assisted CRNs under partial observability, in which distributed secondary users (SUs) jointly select their transmit power and the phase shifts of an assigned subset of IRS elements using only local observations. Primary user (PU) protection is incorporated through an interference-penalized reward, and SUs coordinate by periodically averaging model parameters at a federated server, without exchanging raw observations, channel state information, or replay data. We formulate the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, specify the local learning and aggregation procedure, and characterize its per-round communication cost. Illustrative performance trends contrast FMASAC with centralized SAC, independent SAC, IRS-fixed multi-agent reinforcement learning, and a heuristic CRN strategy. We also outline the simulation-based evaluation and the open challenges, namely constraint handling, agent heterogeneity, and scalability, that are needed to validate the framework.

In contrast, LP-free algorithms only require first-order computations but induce a worse performance. In this work, we bridge the gap between these two extremes by proposing a well-performing algorithm that solves LPs at a few selected time points and conducts first-order computations at other time points. radar.title: Near-Optimal Mechanisms for Resource Allocation Without Monetary Transfers
radar.summary: Aligning Incentives Without Opening the Wallet Many organizations must repeatedly allocate scarce resources—computing capacity, scientific equipment, school seats, or food-bank supplies—when monetary payments are impractical or undesirable. Blanchard and Jaillet show how future allocations can serve as rewards and penalties, inducing strategic agents to report their values truthfully while keeping welfare close to the full-information ideal. Their mechanisms use the promised utility framework and apply to general utility distributions in both finite-horizon and discounted infinite-horizon settings. The key insight is geometric; performance depends on the shape of the attainable-utility frontier. When agents often have similar values for the resource, the planner can shift allocations at little welfare cost and align incentives more effectively. The paper establishes universal convergence guarantees, faster rates for smooth utility distributions, and even exponentially small welfare losses in some discounted settings with frequent ties. The results provide a unified, quantitative framework for deciding when nonmonetary allocation can nearly match mechanisms that use payments.

radar.title: Autonomous AI-Driven Security Operations Centers (Autonomous SOC): Agentic Orchestration, Real-Time Incident Response, and Multi-Agent Defensive Playbooks
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law. Index Terms—Autonomous SOC, Security Operations Center, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), SOAR, Incident Response, MITRE ATT&CK, Dec-POMDP, Defensive AI, Alert Fatigue, Cyber Threat Intelligence.

radar.title: Discrete Single-Parameter Optimal Auction Design
radar.venue_raw: ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation
radar.summary: We study the classic single-item auction setting of Myerson, but under the assumption that the buyers’ values for the item are distributed over finite supports. Using strong LP duality and polyhedral theory, we rederive various key results regarding the revenue-maximizing auction, including the characterization through virtual welfare maximization and the optimality of deterministic mechanisms, as well as a novel, generic equivalence between dominant-strategy and Bayesian incentive compatibility. Inspired by this, we abstract our approach to handle more general auction settings, where the feasibility space can be given by arbitrary convex constraints, and the objective is a linear combination of revenue and social welfare. We characterize the optimal auctions of such systems as generalized virtual welfare maximizers, by making use of their KKT conditions, and we present an analogue of Myerson’s payment formula for general discrete single-parameter auction settings. Additionally, we prove that integrality of the feasibility space is a sufficient condition to guarantee the optimality of auctions with integral allocation rules. Finally, we demonstrate this KKT approach by applying it to a setting where bidders are interested in buying feasible flows on trees with capacity constraints, and provide a combinatorial description of the (randomized, in general) optimal auction.

Are language models rational? The case of coherence norms and belief revision
radar.summary: Do norms of rationality apply to machine learning models, in particular language models? In this paper we investigate this question by focusing on a special subset of rational norms: coherence norms. We consider both logical coherence norms as well as coherence norms tied to the strength of belief. To make sense of the latter, we introduce the Minimal Assent Connection (MAC) and propose a new account of credence, which captures the strength of belief in language models. This proposal uniformly assigns strength of belief simply on the basis of model-internal next token probabilities. We argue that rational norms tied to coherence do apply to some language models but not to others. This issue is significant since rationality is closely tied to predicting and explaining behavior, and thus it is connected to considerations about AI safety and alignment, as well as understanding model behavior more generally.

radar.title: A QMIX-driven routing protocol for dynamic Underwater Acoustic Sensor Networks
radar.summary: Abstract Reliable and energy-efficient data collection remains a fundamental challenge in Underwater Acoustic Sensor Networks (UASNs) owing to limited battery capacity, high propagation delay, dynamic network topology and unreliable communication links. To address these challenges, we propose a Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (CMARL)-based data routing framework for dynamic UASNs. The routing problem is modeled as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP), where each relay node acts as an autonomous routing agent using locally available information. The framework adopts a Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, in which cooperative routing policies are learned using the QMIX algorithm and executed through trained local Q -networks. Each agent constructs its local observation from residual energy, relative forwarding progress towards the sink, estimated link quality and neighboring node availability, while the action space consists of cooperative next-hop selection. A UASN-oriented reward function that jointly optimizes packet delivery reliability, energy efficiency and network lifetime by encouraging reliable packet forwarding and discouraging inefficient routing decisions. Extensive simulation results show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms representative routing protocols across key metrics - packet delivery rate, end-to-end delay, and network lifetime, providing an effective, scalable and intelligent routing solution for next-generation UASNs.

radar.title: Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Coordinated Emergency Building Sweeps
radar.summary: We develop a Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) framework for coordinating emergency responders during building sweeps. The problem is formulated as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) that captures building topology, occupant vulnerability, dynamic hazards, and partial observability. In the six-room office baseline, MADDPG reaches a 134-second sweep time after 5,000 episodes, within 6.3% of the 126-second theoretical optimum and outperforming PPO and DQN. Extensions to a two-story school and a U-shaped warehouse achieve 120 seconds with five responders and 105 seconds with four responders, respectively, with diminishing returns beyond these staffing levels. Under communication failure, coverage remains about 98% while sweep time rises 15–20%; reduced staffing triggers workload redistribution, and dynamic hazards cause threatened areas to be prioritized. Occupancy sensing, mesh networks, and environmental sensing are projected to reduce sweep time by 35–50%. Sensitivity analysis confirms robust performance across realistic parameter ranges.

radar.title: Finite-Time Minimax Bounds and an Optimal Lyapunov Policy in Queueing Control
radar.summary: Finite-Time Guarantees for Scheduling Scheduling underpins modern infrastructure, including data centers, wireless networks, service systems, and graphics processing unit clusters. In these environments, bursty, nonstationary demand and stringent service objectives call for rigorous finite-time performance guarantees. In “Finite-Time Minimax Bounds and an Optimal Lyapunov Policy in Queueing Control,” Liu, Tan, and Xu develop a minimax framework for analyzing finite-time scheduling performance. The framework quantitatively characterizes how the expected total queue length scales with system capacity and variability in arrivals and departures, providing a basis for evaluating and comparing scheduling policies. The authors also introduce LyapOpt, which accounts for both first- and second-order effects in service allocation, whereas MaxWeight optimizes only first-order drift. Under a specific structured condition, LyapOpt achieves optimal finite-time performance while retaining stability guarantees. In contrast, MaxWeight’s finite-time performance scales suboptimally with system parameters. These results clarify the limitations of classical drift-based scheduling and motivate new queueing-control methods with rigorous finite-time guarantees.

radar.title: Prophet Inequalities for a New Class of Overbooking Problems in Container Shipping
radar.summary: A New Class of Overbooking Problems in Container Shipping Industry Container carriers lose billions of dollars each year when shippers reserve slots but fail to show up with the corresponding cargo. This paper studies an online booking problem under a deposit-based mechanism designed to better align incentives and mitigate the costs of overbooking. The authors derive near-optimal online policies for two demand settings: one in which shippers’ no-show behavior is coupled through a spot market, and another in which no-shows are independent. In the coupled setting, a randomized threshold policy guarantees at least 81.9% of clairvoyant profit. In the independent setting, a simple greedy policy is shown to be asymptotically 0.5-optimal as the number of slots tends to infinity. Extensive simulations further demonstrate strong and robust practical performance.

radar.title: A cooperative MARL framework with game-theoretic interpretation for heterogeneous rudder–propeller coordination in ship trajectory tracking
radar.summary: This paper addresses the trajectory tracking problem of underactuated surface ships, with a focus on the coordinated control of rudder and propeller under coupled nonlinear dynamics. Conventional control strategies and single-agent reinforcement learning approaches often struggle to handle the heterogeneous roles of actuators, leading to suboptimal coordination and undesired control oscillations. To improve actuator-level coordination, the rudder and propeller are modeled as two heterogeneous agents within a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework. A cooperative Markov game formulation is used as a modeling and interpretation tool to characterize cross-actuator payoff externalities, rather than as a closed-form equilibrium-solving framework. Based on the centralized training and decentralized execution paradigm, a MATD3-based control scheme is developed, in which each agent learns role-specific policies from local observations while a centralized critic captures the coupling effects of the system. A mixed reward mechanism is further introduced to incorporate limited cross-agent performance information, aiming to encourage more consistent control behaviors without sacrificing task specialization. Simulation studies under multiple trajectories and disturbance conditions demonstrate that the proposed method achieves improved tracking accuracy compared with conventional PID, LADRC, and single-agent reinforcement learning baselines. In addition, the learned policies exhibit smoother actuator commands, indicating a reduction in high-frequency control variations. These results suggest that incorporating simple reward-level interaction can be beneficial for improving coordination in actuator-level control problems. The proposed framework provides a practical multi-agent perspective for rudder–propeller coordination and offers a potential solution for enhancing trajectory tracking performance in underactuated marine systems.
radar.summary_short: This paper addresses the trajectory tracking problem of underactuated surface ships, with a focus on the coordinated control of rudder and propeller under coupled nonlinear dynamics.

radar.title: CALM: Decentralized Control of Cooperative Aerial Manipulation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: Cooperative aerial manipulation is difficult under wind, payload motion, and noisy goal broadcasts because multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are coupled through a shared payload. We present CALM (Cooperative Aerial Learned Manipulation), a decentralized controller for aerial manipulators carrying a basket while tracking a moving ground robot. CALM combines a parameter-shared Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policy, trained using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), with goal estimation, per-UAV Extended State Observers (ESOs), basket-mass estimation, and anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward. The anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward uses estimated goal motion to rotate the formation before position error develops, reducing basket-yaw lag without adding net commanded force. A disturbance-conditioned critic supports centralized training while execution remains decentralized. Across held-out trajectories, CALM achieves lower mean position and orientation errors than all evaluated baselines, including the matched arm baseline (7.68 versus 10.95 cm and 3.3 versus 4.7$^\circ$), the cable-suspended realization, and two model-based controllers. Under unseen full-information-path degradation, CALM remains statistically comparable or superior to the arm baseline. Videos are available at https://petreric.github.io/CALM/.

radar.title: Role-Guided Risk-Aware Attention for Multi-AUV Target-Zone Reaching under Active Defense
radar.summary: Cooperative target-zone reaching by multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) under active defense remains challenging because each vehicle must make sequential guidance decisions under nonlinear hydrodynamics, sonar-limited perception, obstacle constraints, and defender interference. This paper proposes a role-guided risk-aware attention variant of multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG), termed role-guided risk-aware attention MADDPG (RGRA-MADDPG), for attacker-side multi-AUV target-zone reaching under active defense. Different from homogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) policies, the proposed method assigns mission-specific roles to the AUVs, including a Primary Attack AUV, a Coordinated Strike AUV, and a Bait AUV. A role-conditioned attention module is developed to help each AUV selectively emphasize targets, defenders, obstacles, and teammates from local observations, while a risk-prior bias introduces interpretable obstacle-, defender-, and target-related cues into the attention scores. The framework is trained under centralized training and executed through decentralized local policies. Comparative simulations, perturbation tests, mechanism-isolation studies, and physical-response validation are used to evaluate target-reaching success, cooperative behavior, robustness, and command feasibility. Results show that the proposed method improves adversarial target-zone reaching performance over standard MADDPG-based variants while producing differentiated and interpretable multi-AUV tactics.

radar.title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Multi-agent systems of large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding across domains, introducing dynamics not captured by single-agent evaluations. Yet, existing work has mostly contrasted the behavior of a single agent with that of a collective of fixed size, leaving open a central question: How does group size shape dynamics? Here, we move beyond this dichotomy and systematically explore outcomes across the full range of group sizes. We focus on multi-agent misalignment, building on recent evidence that interacting LLMs playing a simple coordination game can generate collective biases absent in individual models. First, we show that collective bias is a deeper phenomenon than previously assessed: Interaction can amplify individual biases, introduce new ones, or override model-level preferences. Second, we demonstrate that group size affects the dynamics in a nonlinear way, revealing model-dependent dynamical regimes. Finally, we develop a mean-field analytical approach and show that, above a critical population size, simulations converge to deterministic predictions that expose the basins of attraction of competing equilibria. These findings establish group size as a key driver of multi-agent dynamics and highlight the need to consider population-level effects when deploying LLM-based systems at scale.

radar.title: Posterior-conditioned multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive cyber defense
radar.summary: Cyber defense increasingly relies on teams of autonomous agents that must act under partial observability while adversaries shift tactics and objectives over time. Standard multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods often overfit to fixed threat models, whereas worst-case robust training can be overly conservative and fail to use observations about the active attack regime. We propose posterior-conditioned MARL, a context-aware framework formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). In addition to its local history, each defender conditions its decentralized policy on a shared attack-context belief, a probabilistic representation of the attack regime inferred online from recent multi-agent interaction trajectories. This belief provides a low-dimensional representation of evolving adversarial behavior and enables coordinated adaptation during execution without test-time policy optimization or retraining. We provide a performance analysis that quantifies how errors in the inferred attack-context belief translate into degraded long-term defense performance, clarifying the tradeoff between robustness and adaptivity. Experiments on the Cyber Autonomy Gym for Experimentation (CybORG) CAGE-4 cyber operations testbed show improved mission reward and adaptability, particularly under mixed and switching attack conditions, compared with domain-randomized, worst-case robust, and hierarchical defense baselines.

radar.title: Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus: A Resilient Coordination Framework for Next-Generation Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
radar.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have moved from singleturn assistants to persistent, tool-using systems that plan, delegate, and cooperate.This shift has produced an explosion of multi-agent system (MAS) frameworks, interoperability protocols, and orchestration patterns, yet production deployments continue to report failure rates far higher than single-agent baselines.This paper synthesizes the current state of AI agents and multi-agent systems as of mid-2026, organizes the coordination design space into a four-part topology taxonomy, and reviews the emerging empirical literature on why multi-agent systems fail.Building on documented gaps, particularly the absence of adaptive, trust-aware coordination in widely used frameworks.We propose Trust-Weighted Adaptive Consensus (TWAC), a coordination-layer mechanism that combines capability-aware sparse shortlisting, an exponentially-weighted per-agent trust ledger, and uncertainty-gated verification.We evaluate TWAC against round-robin and centralized-auction baselines in a controlled simulation across 500 tasks and 30 independent trials.TWAC improves task success rate while reducing communication overhead relative to full-broadcast coordination and lowering cascading-failure rates by more than an order of magnitude.We conclude with future research implications for trust-based coordination in agentic AI systems.

radar.title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
radar.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.

radar.title: Bayesian Learning of Parametric Mean Field Games with Common Noise
radar.summary: We study the inverse problem of recovering unknown parameters governing the dynamics and rewards of Mean Field Games (MFGs) from partial observations of population trajectories, made stochastic by common noise. The observer seeks to recover a consistent parameter $θ$ via Bayesian inference, facing the challenge that evaluating the likelihood requires solving a new Nash equilibrium (NE) for each candidate $θ$. Due to common noise, the mean-field evolution is stochastic and equilibrium policies are population dependent, which makes solving for each parameter computationally expensive. To overcome this, we introduce the Bayesian-Extended Mean Field Game (BE-MFG), whose single NE simultaneously encodes equilibrium policies for all parameters, enabling efficient learning of the conditional density of mean-field trajectories. We formalize parameter consistency and identifiability in MFGs with common noise and investigate conditions under which consistent parameter recovery is guaranteed. On three synthetic environments of various complexity, we recover the ground-truth parameter accurately from a small number of partial, stochastic observations, outperforming an adaptation of inverse reinforcement learning for MFGs. A fourth experiment, on public electricity market data, suggests that the approach can also be applied to real-world data.
radar.summary_short: We study the inverse problem of recovering unknown parameters governing the dynamics and rewards of Mean Field Games (MFGs) from partial observations of population trajectories, made stochastic by common noise.

radar.title: A Blockchain-Driven Stackelberg Game and MILP Algorithmic Framework for Dynamic Pricing in Multi-Agent Microgrid Networks
radar.venue: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Energy Web
radar.venue_raw: EAI Endorsed Transactions on Energy Web
radar.summary: INTRODUCTION: Decentralized coordination and data transparency in multi-agent networks face significant computational and security bottlenecks when performing joint energy and ancillary service trading, particularly due to nonlinear optimization challenges in complex multi-domain environments. OBJECTIVES: This work aims to overcome these bottlenecks by developing an information-driven dynamic pricing framework that enables transparent, autonomous, and computationally efficient multi-agent decision-making. METHODS: The proposed framework integrates Ethereum-based smart contracts deployed on a public ledger to guarantee immutable data interactions and eliminate centralized dispatching. A Stackelberg game model is established to capture upper-lower level decision-making. To solve the resulting highly nonlinear and non-convex game exactly, the problem is transformed into a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model using Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions and the duality theorem, ensuring exact convergence without approximation errors. RESULTS: Simulation results demonstrate the algorithm’s ability to efficiently find the exact Nash equilibrium, converging to a stable state in approximately 12 iterations. The KKT-MILP framework exhibits exceptional scalability, solving a 50-agent system within just 15 seconds and significantly outperforming traditional heuristic algorithms in computational latency. CONCLUSION: The proposed algorithmic framework mathematically ensures transparent and decentralized decision-making while substantially enhancing computational accuracy and overall economic efficiency of the multi-agent system.

radar.title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
radar.summary: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. Coupling this bound across the two players yields recurrences whose effective coefficient scales as 1/(rho_t^X rho_t^Y), preventing unbounded norm growth. We extend the analysis to finitely many simplex learners under a weighted Minty condition and, through the corresponding CFR variant IR-PCFR+, recover analogous guarantees for finite two-player zero-sum perfect-recall extensive-form games under the same full-reach condition as prior work.

radar.title: Why Alternation Speeds Up Counterfactual Regret Minimization?
radar.summary: Solving imperfect-information games at scale rests on counterfactual regret minimization with the regret matching$^{+}$ (RM$^{+}$) update, and a seemingly minor implementation choice accounts for much of its practical speed: alternating the two players' updates, so that the second player responds to the strategy the first player just produced. A widely repeated intuition explains why: seeing the opponent's fresh strategy should act like optimism. We treat this intuition as a testable hypothesis about deterministic two-player zero-sum self-play dynamics and find that its canonical additive form fails an information-matched test. On an analytic witness family we compare alternating RM$^{+}$ against a one-sided predictive RM$^{+}$ that receives the same information channel each round and differs only in where the fresh signal enters, a persistent regret state versus a transient prediction term. Our main result is a dichotomy theorem that reduces trajectory separation to the recurrence of exact-vertex play by the predictive dynamics: under an interior-band assumption on the alternating iterate, either vertex times recur and the profile distance is at least, infinitely often, an explicit constant that our measurements nearly attain, or they terminate. Across the tested self-play regimes, any correct explanation of the alternation speedup must reproduce a staleness cost present at the smallest tested stale fraction, an advantage that persists across seven orders of payoff conditioning, regime crossings of the optimism family, and a measured per-perturbation cost of weakening the injection path that is far steeper for staleness than for partial persistence.
